newsitem.title: CHILE: El Abra assessing stockpiles after accident.
newsitem.headline: El Abra assessing stockpiles after accident.

text.p: El Abra is still assessing how long its stockpiles will last after a fatal accident cut a key conveyor belt, a spokesman for owners Cyprus Amax Minerals Co said.
Cyprus Amax is waiting for Chilean mining safety regulators to return the accident site to the mine's owners so they can begin the task of digging out the belt, which carries copper ore to a crusher.
Until they finish digging out, the crusher and heap leaching pads will survive on stocks piled up at the terminus of the belt, said spokesman Michael Rounds at Cyprus offices in Denver.
Asked how long the stocks might last, he said, "We don't know at this point, and that's part of the assessment."
Rounds said the mine would have to study the size and grades of the stockpiles, which have gone through the primary crusher, to get a clear idea of how long they would last.
The Santiago newspaper El Mercurio quoted the mine's production manager, John Fenn, as saying the mine had only a week's worth of stockpiles.
The site of the accident, which occurred when a tunnel collapsed as workers loaded earth on top of it, was in the hands of Chilean mining regulatory agency Sernageomin.
"We're hoping the authorities release the site back to us today so we can begin the process," of clearing tonnes of debris from the belt, he said.

The mine's west side, known as SXEW, was still in production, he said. El Abra, the world's largest heap leaching operation, made its first cathode only two months ago and was due to hit full production of 225,000 tonnes next year.
Cyprus Amax owns 51 percent of the mine and the rest is owned by Chilean state mining company Codelco.
